subject: Agriculture
title: Seed Patents and Ownership
description: A micro-lesson that makes Seed Patents and Ownership usable.

hook.text: Four companies control 60% of the global seed market. Seeds that were once shared freely are now patented products.

buildup.text: Bayer-Monsanto, Corteva, Syngenta, and BASF dominate. Farmers must buy new seeds each season.

discovery.text: Patent laws prohibit farmers from saving and replanting patented seeds—a practice that sustained agriculture for 10,000 years.

twist.text: Monsanto sued hundreds of farmers for patent infringement—even when wind blew patented pollen onto their fields.

climax.text: The Open Source Seed Initiative is creating 'unpatentable' seeds—freely available, like open-source software.

punchline.text: Seeds were humanity's shared tech. Now they're someone's intellectual property.

quiz.question: What percentage of the global seed market do the top four companies control?

details.summary: Seed patents grant companies exclusive rights over plant varieties and genetic traits. This topic examines how intellectual property in seeds affects farmer autonomy, crop diversity, and the power balance between multinational corporations and smallholder farmers.
details.whyItMatters: Four companies control over 60% of global seed sales. When seeds are patented, farmers cannot save and replant them, creating dependency and raising costs for the world's poorest producers.
takeaways: Patented seeds cannot be legally saved, replanted, or shared by farmers
Just four companies control the majority of global commercial seed sales
Open-source seed initiatives are emerging to keep crop genetics freely accessible

faq.question: How do seed patents affect farmers?
faq.answer: Seed patents prohibit farmers from saving, replanting, or sharing patented seeds without paying royalties. This increases input costs, creates dependency on seed companies, and can lead to legal action against farmers who violate seed agreements.

faq.question: What are open-source seed initiatives?
faq.answer: Open-source seed initiatives release crop varieties under pledges that prevent anyone from patenting them, ensuring genetic material remains freely available for breeding and farming, similar to open-source software licensing.
